Today

  • Topic 7 (Single-Phase Inverters) built the single-phase inverter and its modulation: square-wave, bipolar and unipolar SPWM.
  • Single-phase power balance: the ac side draws a double-frequency (\(2\omega\)) power pulsation that the dc side must supply
  • Sizing the dc-link capacitor to buffer that pulsation for a given voltage ripple
  • Three-phase power balance: the \(2\omega\) terms cancel between phases

Power Balance in Single-Phase Inverters

Assumptions:

  • Ideal ac-side filter: the inverter outputs a pure sinusoidal current with no harmonic content, \(i_t = i_{t,1}\). The PWM voltage \(v_t\) keeps its harmonics; only its fundamental, \(v_{t,1}\), is drawn.
  • Unity power factor: reactive power is zero, so the converter only supplies or absorbs real power.
  • Under these assumptions the instantaneous power flow, and the origin of the twice line-frequency power pulsation in single-phase systems, are clear to see.

Instantaneous Power in Single-Phase Inverters

\[ \begin{aligned}p_{t,1}(t) &= v_{t,1}(t)\,i_t(t)\end{aligned} \]

\[ \begin{aligned}\phantom{p_{t,1}(t)} &= \hat V_{t,1}\cos(\omega t+\theta)\cdot\hat I_{t,1}\cos(\omega t+\theta)\end{aligned} \]

\[ \begin{aligned}\phantom{p_{t,1}(t)} &= \hat V_{t,1}\hat I_{t,1}\cos^2(\omega t+\theta)\end{aligned} \]

\[ \begin{aligned}\phantom{p_{t,1}(t)} &= \tfrac12\hat V_{t,1}\hat I_{t,1}\bigl(1+\cos(2(\omega t+\theta))\bigr)\end{aligned} \]

\[ \begin{aligned}\phantom{p_{t,1}(t)} &= \underbrace{P}_{\text{average}} + \underbrace{P\cos\bigl(2(\omega t+\theta)\bigr)}_{\text{twice line-frequency}}\end{aligned} \]

  • The \(2\omega\) pulsation must be buffered by the dc source, \(v_{d}\): \(i_{d} = \pm i_{t}\) only while \(S_1S_4\) or \(S_2S_3\) conducts, a pulse train averaging \(p_{t,1}/V_{d}\) about \(I_{d} = P/V_{d}\).

Determining Capacitance Requirement

  • In practical applications, there is not a stiff dc voltage source, \(v_{d}\), across the link of the converter, i.e.:

Determining Capacitance Requirement

  • A dc-link capacitor is needed to hold \(v_{d}\) nearly constant, because the source is not stiff.
  • It is the intermediate energy store: it absorbs and releases the difference between the dc-side and ac-side power.

  • Two consequences:

    • The ripple on \(v_{d}\) stays small, and the bridge passes any \(v_{d}\) ripple on to the ac voltage.
    • By KCL, the capacitor supplies the pulsating part of the current the bridge draws, \(i_{d,inv}\), so the source current \(i_{d}\) stays nearly dc.

Determining Capacitance Requirement

\[ p_c(t) = p_t(t) - p_{d}(t) \]

  • With \(p_{d} = P\), the capacitor carries the whole \(2\omega\) term of \(p_{t,1}\), the switching-period average of \(p_t\): it discharges while \(p_{t,1} > P\) and charges while \(p_{t,1} < P\).

P = 5 kW at pf 1 · Vd = 425 V · C = 1 mF · f1 = 60 Hz · unipolar PWM, ma = 0.8 · fsw = 1 kHz, then 10 kHz

Determining Capacitance Requirement

Require ripple \(\le \Delta v_{d}\); \(C\) from the stored energy, \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}C v_{d}^2\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta E &= \tfrac{1}{2}C\Bigl[\underbrace{\bigl(v_{d}+\tfrac{\Delta v_{d}}{2}\bigr)^2}_{v_{d,max}^2}-\underbrace{\bigl(v_{d}-\tfrac{\Delta v_{d}}{2}\bigr)^2}_{v_{d,min}^2}\Bigr] \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2}C\bigl[2v_{d}\,\Delta v_{d}\bigr] = C\,v_{d}\,\Delta v_{d} \end{aligned} \]

\[ \Rightarrow\; C = \frac{\Delta E}{v_{d}\,\Delta v_{d}} \]

\[ \boxed{\,C \ge \frac{P/\omega}{v_{d}\,\Delta v_{d}}\,} \]

Switching ripple neglected: only the \(2\omega\) term sizes \(C\).

\(\Delta E\) from the power pulsation

\[ \Delta E = \int_0^{\pi/2\omega} P\sin(2\omega t)\,dt = \frac{P}{2\omega}\bigl[1-\cos\pi\bigr] = \frac{P}{\omega} \]

Single-Phase Power Balance (Reactive Power Case)

  • Only reactive power: \(i_t\) lags \(v_{t,1}\) by \(90^\circ\), so

\[ \begin{aligned} p_{t,1}(t) &= \hat V_{t,1}\cos(\omega t+\theta)\cdot\hat I_{t,1}\sin(\omega t+\theta)\\ &= Q\sin\bigl(2(\omega t+\theta)\bigr), \qquad Q=\tfrac12\hat V_{t,1}\hat I_{t,1} \end{aligned} \]

  • The average is zero, but the \(2\omega\) pulsation remains: \(C\) must still buffer \(\Delta E = Q/\omega\).
  • In general the \(2\omega\) term has amplitude \(S\):

\[ \begin{aligned} p_{t,1} &= P + P\cos\bigl(2(\omega t+\theta)\bigr) + Q\sin\bigl(2(\omega t+\theta)\bigr)\\ \Rightarrow\; C &\ge \frac{S/\omega}{v_{d}\,\Delta v_{d}}, \qquad S=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2} \end{aligned} \]

Power Balance in Three-Phase Inverters

  • Ideal filter: the inverter outputs a pure sinusoidal current with no harmonic content.
  • Unity power factor: reactive power is zero, so the converter only supplies or absorbs real power.

\[ \begin{aligned} v_{tAN,1} &= \hat V_{t,1}\cos(\omega t+\theta)\\ v_{tBN,1} &= \hat V_{t,1}\cos\bigl(\omega t-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\theta\bigr)\\ v_{tCN,1} &= \hat V_{t,1}\cos\bigl(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\theta\bigr)\\[0.4em] i_{tA} &= \hat I_{t,1}\cos(\omega t+\theta)\\ i_{tB} &= \hat I_{t,1}\cos\bigl(\omega t-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\theta\bigr)\\ i_{tC} &= \hat I_{t,1}\cos\bigl(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\theta\bigr) \end{aligned} \]

Power Balance in Three-Phase Inverters

Recall, per phase: \(p_{tA,1}(t) = v_{tAN,1}(t)\,i_{tA}(t) = P + P\cos\bigl(2(\omega t+\theta)\bigr)\)

Summing the three phases:

\[ p_{t,1}(t) = 3P + P\Bigl[\cos\bigl(2(\omega t+\theta)\bigr) + \cos\bigl(2(\omega t-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\theta)\bigr) + \cos\bigl(2(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\theta)\bigr)\Bigr] \]

Since \(\cos x+\cos\bigl(x-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr)+\cos\bigl(x+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr)=0\):

\[ \Rightarrow\; p_{t,1}(t) = 3P \]

Power Balance in Three-Phase Inverters

  • In three-phase systems, the \(2\omega\) ripple cancels between phases.

  • Consequently, the instantaneous power into the inverter equals the instantaneous power out of the inverter, i.e. \(p_{d}=p_{t,1}\). The implications are:

    • There is no \(2\omega\) power provided by the dc capacitor and therefore no stored-energy requirement, leading to a reduced dc capacitance.
    • A dc capacitor is still required for switching-ripple mitigation.

Representative waveforms (pf = 1)

Power Balance in Three-Phase Inverters (Reactive Power Case)

  • Similarly, in the other extreme case, when only reactive power is being delivered or absorbed by the inverter, the instantaneous power is

\[ p_{t,1}(t) = 0 \quad\text{(as expected)} \]

Representative waveforms (pf = 0)

Power Balance in Three-Phase Inverters (Reactive Power Case)

  1. No real power, so \(I_{d}=0\).
  2. Switching puts harmonics into \(i_{d,inv}\), at \(f_{sw}\) and above.
  3. There \(C\) is the low-impedance path: \(i_{c}\approx i_{d,inv}-I_{d}\).
  4. The source side is high impedance at \(f_{sw}\), so \(i_{d}\approx I_{d}\).
  5. \(i_{d,inv}\), \(i_{c}\) repeat every \(T_1/6\) (dashed): \(6f_1\), not \(2f_1\).

Switching Ripple: What the Capacitor Sees

  • No \(2\omega\) term: the ripple lives within one switching period, \(T_s=1/f_{sw}\).
  • KCL at the dc node, with the source supplying a steady \(I_{d}\):

\[ i_{c} = i_{d,inv}-I_{d} \quad\Rightarrow\quad C\,\frac{dv_{d}}{dt} = I_{d}-i_{d,inv} \]

  • The bridge draws more than \(I_{d}\): \(v_{d}\) falls. Less: \(v_{d}\) rises.
  • Worst case, peak-to-peak (derived later):

\[ \Delta v_{d}\le\frac{\sqrt3}{8}\,\frac{\hat I_{t,1}}{C f_{sw}} \]

Switching Ripple: Worked Example

Given: \(S=5\) kVA (any pf), \(V_{d}=425\) V, \(m_a=0.8\), \(f_1=60\) Hz, \(f_{sw}=10\) kHz, \(\Delta v_{d}=1\,\%\text{ of }V_{d}=4.25\) V peak-to-peak.

Three-phase current

  1. Each phase to \(N\) peaks at \(\hat V_{t,1}=\tfrac{m_a V_{d}}{2}=170\) V, so \(V_{LL}=208\) V rms.
  1. Three phases, each rms \(\times\) rms: \[ S=3\,\frac{\hat V_{t,1}}{\sqrt2}\,\frac{\hat I_{t,1}}{\sqrt2} \;\Rightarrow\;\hat I_{t,1}=\frac{2S}{3\hat V_{t,1}}=19.6\text{ A} \]
  1. Three-phase, worst-case switching ripple: \[ C\ge\frac{\sqrt3}{8}\,\frac{\hat I_{t,1}}{f_{sw}\,\Delta v_{d}}=100\ \mu\text{F} \]
  1. Single-phase, same \(S\), \(V_{d}\), \(\Delta v_{d}\) (\(2\omega\) swing): \[ C\ge\frac{S/\omega}{V_{d}\,\Delta v_{d}}=7.3\text{ mF} \]
  • About 70 times less \(C\) in three-phase.
